## Course Description
Video games have become one of the largest entertainment industries in the world, 
and the software behind them draws on nearly every area of computer science at once. 
Modern real-time games have been used not only for entertainment but also in education, 
simulation, training, and scientific visualization. In this course, we'll explore how modern 
2-D and 3-D interactive games are built, learning the concepts and tools behind them and 
applying them to develop real, playable games. We'll cover core areas including graphics, 
parallel processing, human-computer interaction, networking, artificial intelligence, 
and software engineering, and see how they come together in a single interactive system. 
We will also explore real-world applications of game technology and discuss the social 
and ethical context in which games are developed, marketed, and played.

## Course Goals
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

- explain the social and ethical context in which software and video games are developed, marketed, and used;
- describe the technologies and platforms upon which modern interactive software and video games are built;
- apply software engineering concepts necessary to develop video games within a development team;
- analyze the computational theory used in game design and related fields of computer science (artificial intelligence, computer graphics, networks, etc.);
- apply game theory to multi-player games, decision-making, and artificial intelligence.

# Course Breakdown

## Log Book
(tbd points): To assist you in organizing ideas and commentary about the topics covered in class, each student will
document their work in a log book. The log book will also include in-class prompts and end-of-day reflections.
Each topic has resources related to the content covered in class, consisting of textbook passages from
Game Design Workshop (GDW), articles, and/or videos. You can take notes in your log book, and you are expected to come 
to each class having worked through the assigned material. Log books will be checked randomly throughout the course.
Late work: _no late work will be accepted_.

## Game Analyses
(tbd points): We will be critically analyzing two games over the course of the semester to better understand the mechanics and design decisions 
that lead to good game play. Read more about the games we'll be analyzing by going to Materials > Game Analyses.

## Tutorials
(tbd points): We will be learning one game engine over the course of this class using tutorials. These tutorials will act like 
labs and should be completed and submitted by midnight the day they are introducted. There are completion based. _No late work will be accepted_.

## Game Jams
(tbd points): In place of projects, we will have two game jams. Game Jams are a great way to scope out small ideas for games to see if they are worth
investing more time into. Game jams vary in length, from a couple days to several weeks. Our first game jam will take place over two
sessions the last day of week 2, and will focus on the ideation and paper prototyping stage of game creation. The second game jam will take up
the last two weeks of the course, with various stages and documents due before a final game expo. Each game jam will be completed
in teams. Find more information on the game jam specifics by going to the Materials > Game Jams tab. _No late work will be accepted_. 

## Standards-Based Exams
(tbd points): You will take two exams, each graded using standards-based grading. 
Rather than earning a single overall score, you are assessed on how well you 
demonstrate mastery of individual standards.

Each exam assesses a selection of standards drawn from the 
[Game Design Core Standards](#game-design-core-standards) listed on this page. 
A study guide provided before each exam will tell you exactly which standards it covers, so you know what to prepare.

### How standards are graded
Each standard is scored on an 8-point scale, binned into four levels:

| Level | Meaning | Points |
| :---- | :------ | :----: |
| **P** | Proficient | 8 |
| **S** | Satisfactory | 6 |
| **N** | Not satisfactory | 4 |
| **I** | Incomplete | 0 |

Your exam grade is the combination of your scores across all assessed standards.

### Revising a standard
After you receive your exam back, you may revise any standard you wish to improve. 
Each successful revision bumps that standard up one level: an *I* becomes an *N*, an *N* becomes an *S*, and an *S* becomes a *P*.

To revise a standard, submit a response that addresses all three of the following:

- **What went wrong:** identify the errors you made.
- **How to fix it:** provide the corrected work and the correct reasoning.
- **Reflection:** reflect on the question and what you learned from the mistake.

# Policies and Resources
The mission of this course is to make everyone feel welcome, not only in our classroom, but also in the field of
computer science. If there is any reason you do not feel welcome in this class, please talk to me. If anything is said
to you that makes you feel uncomfortable, please talk to me. If there is any life event that is interfering with your
learning in this class, please talk to me. I may not be able to solve all your problems, but I can direct you to the
right resources on campus.

## Plagiarism & Academic Integrity
Plagiarism, the unacknowledged appropriation of another person’s words or ideas, is a serious academic offense. 
It is imperative that you hand in work that is your own, and that cites or gives credit to others whenever you draw from their work. 
This includes citing prompts when using genAI tools or an internet search. 
Please see St.Olaf’s statements on academic integrity and plagiarism at: https://wp.stolaf.edu/thebook/academic/integrity/. 
See also the description of St.Olaf’s honor system at: https://wp.stolaf.edu/honorcouncil/.

## Computer Science Program Attendance Policy Jterm 2026: 
Attending class is essential for learning the
content of the course, as well as practicing communication and collaboration. Missing class hinders your ability to
achieve these important learning outcomes. That said, you understandably may need to occasionally miss class
due to illness or a scheduling conflict. In these situations, I do not want to judge which absences should count as
“excused” or “unexcused.” So, all absences will be treated equally, since they all result in missing important class
time. Additionally, arriving late disrupts not only your own learning but also your classmates’ ability to engage
fully in class activities. Any tardiness over 5 minutes (subject to instructor adjustment) will also be counted
as an absence. During Jterm, each session (morning and afternoon) will have attendance taken, so missing an entire day of class
equates to two absences.

To reflect the importance of attendance in this course: (1) If you have accrued two absences
without contacting me in advance, I’ll notify your academic advisor and the Dean’s Office by filing an Early
Alert Form to make sure you’re getting the support you need. (2) If you have accrued four absences (whether
or not you contacted me in advance), you must meet with me to discuss your standing in the course and what
you need to do to get back on track for successfully completing the class. (3) If you have accrued nine absences
(whether or not you contacted me in advance), you’ll automatically fail the class. Nine absences means missing
nearly a quarter of all class sessions, indicating that you have not legitimately completed a student-centered
course that requires class engagement. If you do need to miss class, I strongly encourage you to check in with
another student on what you missed, and attend office hours to discuss any questions that you have.
